title: Position vs CFrame
summary: Position is WHERE (a point); CFrame is WHERE + WHICH WAY (point + orientation). Reading Position loses rotation; writing Position on some properties teleports without facing. Pick by whether orientation matters.

explanation.whatItIs: Two answers to 'where is it?': a bare coordinate, or a coordinate with a compass attached.
explanation.whyItExists: Some systems only care about location (distance checks); others must know facing (cameras, shooting, docking models).
whenToUse: Position: distances, spawning without rotation, math-only contexts
CFrame: placing/rotating parts, cameras, anything 'facing' a target, relative offsets
Converting: cf.Position extracts the point; CFrame.new(pos) wraps a point (identity rotation)
whenNotToUse: CFrame for pure scalar distance math — wasteful and confusing
Position when rotation must survive the operation
explanation.mentalModel:
```text
Position = (x, y, z)            a dot on the map
CFrame   = (x, y, z) + facing   a dot holding a compass

Need facing? ─yes→ CFrame
            └─no─→ Position is fine
```
tips: part.CFrame writes both; part.Position writes only location (keeps current rotation)
Vector3 for directions/offsets; promote to CFrame when orienting
commonMistakes: Setting Position expecting re-orientation — it doesn't rotate
Storing CFrames when only a point is needed, then comparing with == (use tolerance)

examples.title: Choosing the right tool
examples.code:
local part = workspace.Part

-- Distance only: Position
local d = (part.Position - workspace.Spawn.Position).Magnitude

-- Move without rotating: Position
part.Position = part.Position + Vector3.new(0, 5, 0)

-- Move AND face the player: CFrame
local target = workspace.Dummy.Position
part.CFrame = CFrame.lookAt(part.Position, target)

-- Extract point from pose:
local justThePoint = part.CFrame.Position
